new_statements.quote: 2.3. Prosody. There are 4 contrastive tones in Kaliko viz. Low, Mid, High and Rising (the latter being fairly marginal), as shown in the following examples: contrast Low/Mid ... contrast High/Low: ba (person) ba (house, village) ... contrast Low/Mid/Rising: mba ('he has gone up') mba ('it has grown') mba (moon). [p. 48] ... It should be observed that (i) and (ii) above are responsible for the creation of the phonemic contour tone in Kaliko (Rising Tone; LH) as well as the emergence of a rather marginal Falling Tone (HL). That is, vowels may be deleted or devocalized but the tones associated with them do not disappear. [p. 49]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kaliko (Omi) is described as a register tone language with three level tones (Low, Mid, High) plus a marginal rising contour created by vowel deletion; the description's only prosody section is about tone and it contains no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule is stated). Tone diacritics in the scanned are unreliable; the page images carry the marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone illustrated on citation forms (verb infinitives in -za and nouns); the article's data are one speaker from Ombatse, Oct. 1983.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened primary description is Goyvaerts 1986, whose data are 'Kaliko' of Ombatse village (3.18N 30.40E, c. 70 km N of Aru, Zaire), one speaker, Oct. 1983. Glottolog assigns this to Omi [omi] ('Ombatse... probably = Omi'); the Boone & Watson 1999 survey treats Zairean Kaliko as Kaliko-Omi + Kaliko-Ma'di, both in the collectivite d'Omi, and Ombatse lies near the Glottolog Omi centroid (3.25N 30.54E). Sudanese Keliko is a separate Glottolog language, keli1248 [kbo]; Tucker 1940's Keliko section concerns that variety, not Omi.
